hints: Add the charge on the central iron ion to the total charge from the six $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands to find the overall charge in each case.
walkthrough:
Work out the total ligand charge**
Think of a complex formula as a simple sum. Each $\text{CN}^{-}$ carries a $1-$ charge and there are six of them, so the ligands contribute $6 \times (-1) = -6$ in both A and B.

Add the metal charge**
Now add the iron oxidation state. For A: $(+3) + (-6) = -3$, so you get $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$. For B: $(+2) + (-6) = -4$, so you get $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$. Always show the charge outside the square brackets.

Final answer: complex ion A: $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$
complex ion B: $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$

hints: Recall where the colour of a transition metal complex comes from, splitting of the 3d orbitals and promotion of a d electron by absorbing visible light.
Compare $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ in A with $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in B and think how the different charge and d electron count changes the size of the splitting, $\Delta E$.
walkthrough:
Remember why complexes are coloured**
Picture the five 3d orbitals on iron. When six $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands approach, the d orbitals split into two sets with an energy gap called $\Delta E$. A d electron can jump across this gap by absorbing exactly $\Delta E$ of energy from visible light. The colour you see is the light left over, the complement of what was absorbed.

See why Fe(III) and Fe(II) split differently**
A and B have the same ligands and coordination number, but the metal is different: $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is $3\text{d}^5$ while $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is $3\text{d}^6$, and the higher $3+$ charge pulls ligands closer and polarises them more. That changes the amount of splitting, so $\Delta E$ is different for A and B.

Link different gap to different colour**
Because $\Delta E = hf = hc/\lambda$, a different gap means a different frequency and wavelength is absorbed. If A absorbs one part of the spectrum and B absorbs another part, the transmitted light that reaches your eye is different, so the solutions look different colours.

Final answer: The two ions have different $\Delta E$, the energy gap between the split d orbitals.
They therefore absorb light of different frequency / wavelength from the visible spectrum, so different colours are transmitted / observed.

hints: Think about who supplies both electrons for the bond between the ligand lone pair on carbon and the vacant orbital on $\text{Fe}^{3+}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the lone pair donor**
Every ligand to metal bond works the same way. The carbon atom of $\text{CN}^{-}$ has a lone pair, and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ has vacant 3d / 4s / 4p orbitals. Both electrons in the bond come from the carbon, donated into the empty orbital on iron. When one atom provides both shared electrons, we call it a dative covalent or coordinate bond.

hints: Use the coordination number to predict the shape: 6 ligands is octahedral, 2 ligands is linear, 4 ligands can be tetrahedral or square planar as stated.
Recall the characteristic bond angle for each shape: $90^{\circ}$ for octahedral and square planar, $180^{\circ}$ for linear, $109.5^{\circ}$ for tetrahedral.
Remember to show three dimensions clearly with solid wedges for bonds coming out and hashed wedges for bonds going back, especially for octahedral and tetrahedral.
Check the ligand formulas: six $\text{CN}^{-}$ around Fe, two $\text{NH}_3$ around Ag, four CO around Ni bonded through C, four $\text{Cl}^{-}$ around Pd.
walkthrough:
Draw complex A as octahedral**
Place Fe in the centre and put six $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands around it, four in a plane with one above and one below. Use one wedge and one hashed bond for the axial ligands to show 3D shape. Label any adjacent $\text{C}-\text{Fe}-\text{C}$ angle as $90^{\circ}$. The formula is $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ from part (a)(i).

Draw Ag with ammonia as linear**
Silver(I) here has coordination number 2: $[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^{+}$. Draw $\text{H}_3\text{N}-\text{Ag}-\text{NH}_3$ in a straight line with Ag in the middle. Label the $\text{N}-\text{Ag}-\text{N}$ angle as $180^{\circ}$. No wedges are needed because it is flat.

Draw Ni with CO as tetrahedral**
Nickel(0) with four CO gives $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]$. Put Ni in the centre with four C bonded CO groups pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. Use a wedge for one bond and a hashed bond for another to show depth. Label any $\text{C}-\text{Ni}-\text{C}$ angle as $109.5^{\circ}$. Remember bonding is $\text{Ni}-\text{C}\equiv\text{O}$.

Draw Pd with chloride as square planar**
Palladium(II) with four $\text{Cl}^{-}$ gives $[\text{PdCl}_4]^{2-}$. Draw Pd in the centre with four $\text{Cl}$ ligands at the corners of a square in one plane. Label any adjacent $\text{Cl}-\text{Pd}-\text{Cl}$ angle as $90^{\circ}$. Keep all bonds in the plane, no wedges needed, to contrast it with tetrahedral.

Final answer: complex ion A: octahedral Fe with six $\text{CN}$ ligands, $90^{\circ}$ labelled.
$\text{Ag}^{+}$ with ammonia: linear $\text{H}_3\text{N}-\text{Ag}-\text{NH}_3$, $180^{\circ}$ labelled.
Ni with carbon monoxide: tetrahedral Ni with four CO ligands bonded via C, $109.5^{\circ}$ labelled.
$\text{Pd}^{2+}$ with chloride: square planar Pd with four $\text{Cl}$ ligands, $90^{\circ}$ labelled.
